source: Harris and Slivkins (2026) Should You Use Your Large Language Model to Explore or Exploit? (Sec 3, exploration oracle)
finding: On text-labelled tasks with very many arms, one LLM call that proposes a few candidate arms to explore beats random and genre/retrieval baselines. This is the closest test of 'what is worth trying here' on a text task, with UCB1 run over the proposed arms.
numbers: MovieLens (943 users, 5 reruns): Qwen-2.5 rew 671.88 (K=10) and 678.25 (K=19); Mistral-7B 735.38 and 675.16; random subset 570.39 and 599.73; genre-based 617.27 (K=19). Q/A task (10 open questions, 10 runs): LLMs rew 0.5-0.6, best at K=3 or 4; Random rew < 0.1. arXiv-title task (41 categories x 10 abstracts, 5 reruns): GPT-4o rew about 0.63-0.83 at K=1,2,5, versus MMR retrieval baseline (K=5) about 0.39-0.52. Results similar across prompting strategies (all-at-once vs one-by-one, with or without a diversity nudge) and models (GPT-4o, Qwen-2.5, Gemma-3, Mistral-7B).
quote: LLMs are useful as exploration oracles that propose high-quality candidate actions in large, semantically meaningful action spaces.
limits: Reward is cosine similarity to a known target or a rating table, so the grader is cheap and the action space is semantic. The comparison is to random and retrieval baselines, not to plain repeated sampling or a novelty tie-break at equal tokens. One LLM call per task, not an interactive loop. Knowledge cutoff late 2023 for the models, so the authors used arXiv papers after June 2024.
agent_relevance: Supports S3 as a source of a small, diverse, high-value candidate set when the option space is semantic and large. Does not show gain over plain sampling or over a novelty rule on reasoning tasks.

source: Harris and Slivkins (2026) Should You Use Your Large Language Model to Explore or Exploit? (Sec 2, exploitation and mitigations)
finding: Current LLMs (GPT-5.2, GPT-5-mini, GPT-4o, Qwen, Gemma-3, Mistral, DeepSeek-R1-distill) exploit well on small contextual-bandit puzzles but degrade as size grows. Reasoning models do best but are slow and costly. Summaries and a code interpreter help on linear tasks, yet every LLM stays below simple linear regression, even on non-linear text puzzles.
numbers: CB puzzle d=K=2, T=4000, temp 0, GPT-4: summarising mitigations give FracCorrect about 80-90% without CoT and 60-85% with CoT. GPT-4o d=K=5, T=1000: k-means summary near random guessing; k-nearest about 50%; k-means plus k-nearest about 60%. Text-based non-linear puzzle: linear baseline 70% FracCorrect and all LLM configurations significantly below it; GPT-4o with code interpreter worst. One GPT-4 run with code interpreter cost about 70 USD and 6+ hours, versus a few dollars and under 5 minutes without it.
limits: Exploitation, not tally-based exploration. The authors write that LLMs that fail out of the box 'can be prompted to do so by providing succinct summary statistics' (citing Krishnamurthy), and that such statistics do not exist for contextual bandits. The paper has a 2026 UAI version (v4); earlier versions list different model sets.
agent_relevance: A summary state helps but is not enough on contextual tasks; reasoning models are strongest yet expensive. Supports keeping a tally but not trusting the LLM to do numeric inference itself. Relevant to gap 3 and gap 10 indirectly.

source: Pan, Xie and Wilson (2025) Large Language Models Think Too Fast To Explore Effectively
finding: In the open-ended Little Alchemy 2 game, ordinary LLMs explore worse than humans, but reasoning models (o1, DeepSeek-R1) explore better than humans. Ordinary LLMs rely on uncertainty (novelty) and almost ignore empowerment (which items lead to many new items); o1 uses both.
numbers: 500 trials per run; 5 repetitions per temperature (0, 0.3, 0.7, 1.0; o1 fixed at 1). Elements discovered: LLaMA3.1-8B 9; LLaMA3.1-70B 25; GPT-4o 35; DeepSeek-R1 85; o1 177; humans 42 on average within 500 trials (29,493 players, 4,691,033 trials). o1 vs humans t=9.71, p<0.001; R1 t=3.40; GPT-4o t=-5.48; 70B t=-6.39; 8B t=-28.12. Empowerment weights near zero for most LLMs, highest for o1 (above humans).
limits: One game with a known combination graph, where words carry semantics. Small number of runs per cell. Sparse-autoencoder analysis was done on open models only. R1 and o1 are different training recipes, so the effect is 'reasoning-trained', not one cause.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 10: a reasoning-trained model already explores much better by itself, so an S3 prior step adds least for such models and most for plain chat models. Also shows novelty-only (uncertainty) behaviour is the default failure.

source: Pan, Xie and Wilson (2025) Large Language Models Think Too Fast To Explore Effectively (Appendix C, prompt engineering)
finding: Adding explicit guidance to GPT-4o's prompt (chain of thought, self-reflection, an explicit strategy hint to be diverse and forward-looking) did not significantly improve exploration. The model kept repeating combinations.
numbers: GPT-4o temperature 1, prompt-engineered: average inventory 43 elements versus 35 baseline; t=-1.17, p=0.304 (not significant). Activation steering also did not help significantly.
limits: The prompt did not contain an explicit tried/untried tally of past combinations; the history was already in the trial log. So this is a test of strategy hints, not of a summary state. One model, one game, 2024 model.
agent_relevance: Cautions that a prompt-only hint to 'explore' is weak on a chat model; supports O (explicit operator that forces an untried choice) over advice text. Does not settle gap 3.

source: Lu, Hu and Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models (Game of 24, main result and cost)
finding: An archive of states plus LLM choice of which state to expand and which action to try solves a maths reasoning task (Game of 24) far better than naive LLM, ReAct and Reflexion, at an equal number of environment operations. It needs the ability to return to an archived state.
numbers: 100 hard problems: IGE reaches 100% success in 150 operations, on average 70.8% faster than the best baseline (depth-first search); chi-square p<0.05 at 150 operations. Baselines plateau and are beaten by plain DFS. Tree of Thoughts reported 74% under its own budget. Table 3 (GPT-4): naive 70, ReAct 82, Reflexion 83, IGE 100. API cost per task with GPT-4: Game of 24 1.04 USD, BabyAI 2.01, TextWorld 1.28; total paper cost under 2,000 USD. TextWorld Coin Collector: IGE the only method to solve it; Cooking Game: IGE beats ReAct by 36 points.
quote: assuming an agent can return to a previously discovered state by restoring in the simulator
limits: Comparison is at equal environment operations, not equal tokens; IGE makes extra LLM calls for state selection, filtering and action choice per step. Tokens per success are not reported. Authors assume the agent can restore any archived state in a simulator and say this may be relaxed 'by simply prompting the model with a past trajectory', which they do not test. Same lab as OMNI (Clune).
agent_relevance: For gap 5: the archive helps on a text reasoning task, but only where states can be revisited; a no-reset agent needs the trajectory-in-prompt variant that the authors only mention. Token cost is the open number.

source: Lu, Hu and Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models (Table 2 ablation, Table 4 archive size)
finding: Each LLM-driven piece matters, and which one matters depends on task depth. On the short-horizon Game of 24 the action choice and the per-state action history matter most; on long-horizon text games state selection and archive filtering matter most. Filtering keeps the archive small.
numbers: Success % (mean +/- 95% CI), Game of 24 at 150 steps, 100 seeds: full IGE 100; random action choice 68 +/- 9; random state choice 96 +/- 3.5; no archive filtering 93 +/- 5; all three random 61 +/- 9.5; no state-conditional action history 33 +/- 9; classic Go-Explore with visitation counts 38 +/- 22. BabyAI Put-Next-To (25 seeds): full 84; random state selection 24; no filtering 48. Archive size without filter: Game of 24 18.5 vs 15.6 with filter; BabyAI-Text 203.5 vs 25.5 states; TextWorld Cooking 22.4 vs 4.4. (Some table cells were garbled in extraction; the Game of 24 column and the archive-size ratios were read from text and cross-checked.)
limits: The action-history ablation is the closest published test of a 'tried before in this state' tally: removing it cost 67 points on Game of 24 (100 to 33). Small seed counts on BabyAI and TextWorld (25). Some other cells of Table 2 are uncertain after text extraction.
agent_relevance: The tried/untried list is the single most valuable memory piece on a short-horizon reasoning task (supports gap 3 positively, but with GPT-4-Turbo). Filtering the archive keeps the token cost bounded.

source: Lu, Hu and Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models (Table 3 model choice, Table 5 domain-general prompts)
finding: IGE's gain holds across foundation models and survives weaker, generic prompts, but the size of the gain depends on the model, and the drop with generic prompts varies by task: small on Game of 24, 12 to 20 points on the two text games.
numbers: Game of 24 success %: GPT-4 naive 70, ReAct 82, Reflexion 83, IGE 100; Llama-3 400B 44, 68, 54, IGE 98; Claude Sonnet 3.5 24, 58, 80, IGE 86 (not significantly better than Reflexion). Domain-general prompts: Game of 24 IGE 96 (vs 100); BabyAI Put-Next-To 84 to 68; TextWorld Cooking 92 to 72; ReAct on BabyAI 48 to 24.
limits: Prompt change is a drop in domain detail, not a paraphrase test. Models are 2024-era. No frontier reasoning model.
agent_relevance: Bears on gaps 4 and 10: gains from archive plus LLM choice stay large on a strong non-reasoning model (Claude 3.5 naive 24 to 86). Loss of prompt detail costs up to 20 points on interactive text games.

source: Bougie and Watanabe (2025) Exploring Beyond Curiosity Rewards: Language-Driven Exploration in RL (iLLM) (Table 3, Atari)
finding: Recovered the Atari table. iLLM(hop) beats the curiosity baselines on four of five hard-exploration games; on Seaquest it is slightly below APT. Pitfall 125 is confirmed. Only 10 seeds, and the LLM is a small Transfo-XL (280M), not a modern LLM.
numbers: Score at 100M steps, 10 seeds, mean +/- std. Montezuma's Revenge: RND 456 +/- 55, NGU 512 +/- 39, APT 711 +/- 66, ChibiT 1,231 +/- 187, iLLM(hop) 2,632 +/- 277. PrivateEye: RND 598, NGU 1,872, APT 2,982, ChibiT 3,633, iLLM(hop) 4,422 +/- 376. Gravitar: RND 192, NGU 1,630, APT 1,420, ChibiT 2,983, iLLM(hop) 4,044 +/- 559. Pitfall: RND -11, NGU -6, APT -12, ChibiT -10, iLLM(hop) 125 +/- 24. Seaquest: RND 2,612, NGU 15,616, APT 19,989, ChibiT 16,441, iLLM(hop) 18,851 +/- 2,930. ELLM and iLLM(obs) could not be run (no text observations).
limits: Human-meaningful-exploration table: iLLM(hop) trajectories are closer to human demonstrations than PPO and RND. Atari games are familiar to LLMs via text; unfamiliarity was not varied. Authors are the method's authors.
agent_relevance: Closes the 'real numbers' gap (gap 7) for Atari. The gain is largest in well-known Montezuma and absent on Seaquest; weak, uncontrolled evidence on gap 8.

source: Bougie and Watanabe (2025) Exploring Beyond Curiosity Rewards: Language-Driven Exploration in RL (iLLM) (Tables 1, 2, MiniHack and BabyAI)
finding: iLLM beats ELLM and curiosity baselines in MiniHack, except on the hardest tasks where all methods stay low. The authors say LLM mistakes cap ELLM; ELLM also scores lower in BabyAI because goal-achievement checking is hard and it picks poor goals.
numbers: MiniHack success (10 runs): LavaCrossing-Ring iLLM(hop) 0.97 +/- 0.02 at 28M steps, iLLM(obs) 1.0 at 22M, best other listed 0.98 +/- 0.10 (35M); LavaCross-Potion 0.99-1.0; LavaCross-Full 0.98-1.0 (best baseline 0.50); MultiRoom-N4-Monster 0.75 +/- 0.07 for iLLM(hop), 0.72 for obs, best baseline 0.70; River-Monster iLLM(hop) 0.38 +/- 0.12 vs best listed baseline 0.22 +/- 0.03, iLLM(obs) 0.13. RND and NGU are 0.0 on all five tasks. BabyAI PickUpLoc: iLLM(hop) about 0.85 after 68M steps while RND and NGU stay under 0.25 after 100M.
limits: Method rows in the PMLR text extraction are not labelled, so the baseline-to-number mapping for non-iLLM rows is inferred from order and from the paper's prose. The iLLM River-Monster value (0.38) is the last row; the 0.22 comparison value is probably but not surely PAE. ELLM is reported as capped in these tasks.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 9: a second lab re-ran ELLM as a baseline on different games with a different LLM and found it weaker than its own method. That is not a replication of ELLM's own claims. Hard sparse tasks (River-Monster) stay unsolved.

source: Bougie and Watanabe (2025) Exploring Beyond Curiosity Rewards: Language-Driven Exploration in RL (iLLM) (Table 5 noisy TV, Table 4 backbone, Table 7 dense reward)
finding: In a noisy-TV test (GoToObj with a random-noise patch or random actions) all curiosity baselines drop and iLLM drops less. The backbone changes the score only slightly. With dense rewards iLLM does not hurt.
numbers: GoToObj success (10 seeds): Original: RND 0.51, NGU 0.42, ELLM 0.66, APT 0.48, ChibiT 0.56, iLLM(obs) 0.94, iLLM(hop) 0.92. Noise patch: RND 0.24, NGU 0.16, ELLM 0.45, APT 0.22, ChibiT 0.41, iLLM(obs) 0.65, iLLM(hop) 0.59. Noise action 0.05: ELLM 0.58, iLLM 0.91; 0.10: ELLM 0.55, ChibiT 0.66, iLLM(obs) 0.87. Paired t-tests p<0.002 for the noise-action settings. Backbone average return over nine BabyAI tasks: Transfo-XL 0.83-0.85, Flan-T5 0.75-0.79, Llama-2 7B 0.87-0.88. Dense-reward BabyAI: PPO 0.12/0.0/0.16/0.0 vs iLLM 0.90/0.46-0.52/0.90/0.72-0.75.
limits: At noise action 0.10 ChibiT (0.66) beats ELLM and stays within about 0.2 of iLLM. Baselines are curiosity methods and ELLM; no LLM-free tie-break. Randomised-TV is the standard noisy-TV problem, not a test of an interestingness filter.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 7 for the noisy-TV table. LLM-based priors reduce the noisy-TV failure of a pure novelty bonus, which supports a prior-plus-novelty combination in S3.

source: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov and Suhr (2024) Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design (FormatSpread)
finding: Meaning-preserving changes in prompt format (separators, casing, spacing) change accuracy a lot, in open models and API models, and size, few-shot examples and instruction tuning do not remove it. Format performance correlates only weakly between models.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points spread for LLaMA-2-13B across plausible formats; average spread about 10 points across 50+ tasks and several models; GPT-3.5 spread up to 56 points, median 6.4 points across 320 formats.
limits: About classification-style few-shot tasks and formatting (not paraphrasing a request for probes), mostly 2023 models. Newer RLHF and reasoning models were not tested in this paper. Says nothing about exploration prompts.
agent_relevance: General evidence for gap 4: wording and format can move results by tens of points on older models. Nobody has measured it for 'what is worth trying' prompts, so test our own S3 prompt over a set of paraphrases and report the range.

source: Zhang, Diddee, Holm et al. (2025) NoveltyBench: Evaluating Language Models for Human-like Diversity
finding: Plain repeated sampling from aligned LLMs returns near-duplicates; asking the model again while showing its earlier answers in context restores human-level diversity. System-prompt encouragement and paraphrasing barely help.
numbers: 20 models; frontier models give fewer than 3 distinct answers on average in 10 samples; Claude 3, Gemini and GPT-4o score below 4 out of 10 on cumulative utility; small models (Gemma 2 2B, Llama 3.2 1B) show the highest diversity. On 100 curated prompts, with 8 generations: in-context regeneration brings Claude-3 Opus, GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro roughly to the diversity of 8 human authors; GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro exceed the humans on cumulative utility. Equivalence classifier 79% agreement with human labels.
limits: Open-ended creative and subjective prompts, not reasoning tasks with a right answer. The human baseline is the paper authors (a lower bound). Regeneration is sequential, so token cost grows with the number of answers.
agent_relevance: For gap 1: the right comparison for 'ask what is worth trying' is not independent sampling but a sequential 'show what you already proposed' loop, the same idea as a tried/untried list. Plain sampling is a weak baseline.

source: Zhang, Yu, Chong et al. (2026) Verbalized Sampling: How to Mitigate Mode Collapse and Unlock LLM Diversity
finding: Asking for several responses with stated probabilities in a single prompt gives more diverse output than direct, sequence or multi-turn prompting, without a clear quality loss, and more capable models gain more. Using the diverse set to make training problems also raised downstream maths accuracy.
numbers: Creative writing: diversity 1.6 to 2.1 times direct prompting; larger models (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Pro) gain 1.5 to 2 times more than small ones. Human ratings (1-4 scale): poem direct 1.90, sequence 2.07, VS 2.39; story 2.74, 2.76, 3.06; joke 1.83, 2.93, 3.01. Synthetic maths data (1K questions generated, then SFT): average accuracy over MATH500, OlympiadBench and Minerva: baseline 32.8, direct 30.6, sequence 33.7, VS-Standard 36.1, VS-CoT 37.5, VS-Multi 36.9 (GPT-4.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash generators pooled).
limits: Diversity measured by embeddings and human raters on creative tasks. No test of whether the diverse candidates are more useful in an exploration loop. Sequence and VS-Standard cost some quality on small models.
agent_relevance: Gives a cheap S3 prompt form: ask for K candidates with probability labels and sample the low-probability ones. Needs a test on our tasks; it is a better plain-sampling baseline than temperature.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: When an LLM is asked what is worth trying (research ideas), expert reviewers judge its ideas more novel than expert-written ones but slightly less feasible. The LLM keeps repeating itself, and LLM judges cannot rank ideas reliably.
numbers: Blind review by 79 experts, 49 ideas per condition (about 109-119 reviews per arm): mean novelty human 4.84, AI 5.64 (AI + human rerank 5.81), significant after correction; excitement 4.55 vs 5.19 (5.46); feasibility human 6.61, AI 6.34 (reranked 6.44), not significant; expected effectiveness 5.13 vs 5.47. Duplication: out of 4,000 generated seed ideas per topic only about 5% (about 200) remain after de-duplication at cosine 0.8. LLM-as-judge accuracy on balanced top/bottom 25% ideas: 45-54% across GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 pairwise or direct scoring versus human inter-reviewer consistency 56.1%.
limits: Research-idea writing with NLP researchers as reviewers, not an exploration loop with outcomes. Nobody ran the ideas; an execution study was only proposed. Subjective ratings.
agent_relevance: Best text-domain evidence for gap 2: proposals are not much less feasible than expert ones (6.34 vs 6.61), but the model repeats itself and cannot grade its own proposals. A feasibility filter by the same model should not be assumed to work (see d16).

source: Valmeekam, Stechly and Kambhampati (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? A Preliminary Evaluation of OpenAI's o1 on PlanBench
finding: Plans from LLMs are often invalid, and validity collapses when the domain is disguised by renaming. This is a controlled familiarity test: the same problems are solved at up to 62.6% when familiar and under 5% when obfuscated. Reasoning models close much of the gap but not all.
numbers: 600 Blocksworld instances (3-5 blocks): best LLM LLaMA 3.1 405B 62.6% zero-shot; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 57.6% one-shot; GPT-4o 35.5% zero-shot. Mystery Blocksworld (same problems with obfuscated names): no LLM reaches 5%; giving GPT-4 the translation reaches only 10%. o1-preview 97.8% Blocksworld, 52.8% Mystery zero-shot (one-shot 41.6%); o1-mini 56.6% and 19.1%; Fast Downward planner 100% in 0.265 s versus o1-preview 40 to 83 s.
limits: Planning with exact validity, not exploration. Preliminary: o1-preview and o1-mini only, a week after release. Only Blocksworld variants.
agent_relevance: For gaps 2 and 8: an LLM's competence depends strongly on surface familiarity, so LLM priors should be trusted less when the task is renamed or novel. Argues for a cheap external validity check (a rule checker) where one exists.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: When the same model checks and corrects its own answer without outside feedback, accuracy stays flat or drops. With an oracle label, correction helps a lot. So a 'cheap feasibility check' done by the same LLM cannot be assumed to recover proposal losses.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic self-correction: GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 (round 1) to 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 95.5 and GPT-4 97.5. In 74.7% of GSM8K cases GPT-3.5 keeps its first answer; changes go more often from right to wrong.
limits: Self-correction of answers, not feasibility of a proposed probe. 2023 models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2). Reasoning-trained models were not tested.
agent_relevance: Supports G (verify with something external, a check that can fail) over self-judgement for gap 2. A rule check or a run result recovers the loss, not a second look by the same model.

source: Wang, Liu, Xu et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Reasoning-trained models search internally, but they switch from one line of thought to another too early, especially on hard problems and when they fail. Penalising thought-switch tokens at decoding improved accuracy without further training. So internal search is real but not well directed.
numbers: AIME2024 and other sets: o1-like models (QwQ-32B-Preview, DeepSeek-R1 variants) use on average 225% more tokens on incorrect than correct responses, with 418% more thought switches; ordinary LLMs show no such length difference. Thought-switch penalty (TIP) gave a few points of accuracy on AIME2022-23 (grid of penalty strength and duration, about 35 to 40 pass@1 for QwQ-Preview depending on setting).
limits: Open models from 2024 to early 2025 on maths. The effect is on decoding, not prompts. Whether a visible tried-list in the prompt reduces switching is untested here.
agent_relevance: For gap 10: S3 is not obviously redundant for reasoning models, because they explore too shallowly and without a record of what was tried; a tally or 'finish this branch' rule may still add value. No direct test.

source: Pan, Xie and Wilson (2025) Large Language Models Think Too Fast To Explore Effectively (reasoning traces)
finding: The reasoning model (DeepSeek-R1) writes long iterative traces that keep revisiting past trials and combinations; GPT-4o with chain of thought writes short, less detailed ones. The authors link this to R1's better exploration. In open models, uncertainty is encoded in early layers and empowerment later, which they argue makes chat models decide too early.
numbers: Elements found: R1 85 vs GPT-4o 35 (500 trials). Higher temperature changes uncertainty-driven choices only (beta=2.911, z=7.440, p<0.001) and not empowerment (beta=0.196, z=1.067, p=0.286). Sparse-autoencoder analysis took 42 hours on a V100.
limits: The mechanistic part is on open models and correlational. Trace features measured on one task.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that sampling temperature alone is a poor way to get directed exploration, so the S3 operator should pick on a stated reason (empowerment-like value) and not only on novelty.
